 Corporate Responsibility in India – Jobs, Wages and Domestic Manufacturing
 Prime Minister Modi discussed key aspects of corporate responsibility in India at the centenary celebrations of FICCI.

 Corporate Responsibility Latest News 
 Prime Minister Narendra Modi criticised India Inc at the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) centenary celebrations on November 19, 2026, questioning the failure of corporates to translate tax benefits and ease-of-doing-business reforms into higher employee salaries, greater employment and better-quality products. 
 Background: Prime Minister’s Message to India Inc 
 Addressing business leaders at FICCI’s centenary event at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, the Prime Minister questioned whether the private sector had adequately contributed to employment generation and wage growth despite receiving significant policy support from the government. 
 He highlighted that the corporate tax rate had been reduced from 30% in 2014 to 22% in 2019, while income up to Rs. 12 lakh had effectively become tax-free under the new tax regime, subject to applicable conditions. 
 However, he argued that these measures had not been matched by comparable increases in employee salaries or the number of people employed by companies.  
 He criticised businesses for retaining the gains rather than passing them on to employees and consumers. 
 The Prime Minister also questioned the quality of products manufactured for Indian consumers, arguing that the size of India’s domestic market should not become an excuse for compromising on quality. 
 ‹ 
 › 
 Corporate Profits and the Wage-Growth Gap 
 The criticism comes amid evidence of rising corporate profitability alongside concerns over wage stagnation and the quality of employment. 
 Corporate earnings: Nifty-500 companies recorded a 28.7% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) in earnings between FY2020 and FY2026, compared with 9.5% CAGR for India’s GDP. 
 Profitability: The Reserve Bank of India’s March 2026 assessment found that the aggregate profits of 7,992 non-government, non-financial public limited companies increased by 23.1% in FY2024-25. Their combined profits rose from Rs. 2.5 trillion in FY2020-21 to Rs. 7.1 trillion in FY2024-25. 
 Profit-to-GDP ratio: The corporate profit-to-GDP ratio for Nifty-500 companies reached 5.2% in FY2025-26, an all-time high, while the ratio for listed Indian companies stood at 5.7%, an 18-year high. 
 Direct tax composition: Personal income-tax collections, including Securities Transaction Tax (STT), reached Rs. 10.45 lakh crore in FY2023-24, exceeding corporate tax collections of Rs. 9.11 lakh crore. 
 These figures highlight the growing debate over the distribution of economic gains between businesses, employees and the government. 
 Employment Growth and the Quality of Jobs 
 According to the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) , the Worker Population Ratio (WPR) for people aged 15 years and above increased from 46.8% in 2017-18 to 58.2% in 2023-24. The unemployment rate declined from 6% to 3.2% during the same period. 
 However, higher employment does not necessarily translate into the creation of secure, formal-sector jobs. 
 Informal employment: A NITI Aayog report based on PLFS 2023-24 data estimated that nearly 87% of India’s 63.4 crore employed workers were in informal employment, with only around 13% in formal jobs. 
 Skill mismatch: The Economic Survey 2024-25 found that more than 53% of graduates and around 36% of postgraduates were employed in occupations below their educational qualifications. 
 Job security: A significant proportion of workers remain outside the organised workforce and lack benefits such as medical insurance and provident fund coverage. 
 Improving Product Quality and Consumer Protection 
 The Prime Minister also criticised manufacturers for relying on India’s large domestic consumer base rather than investing sufficiently in product quality. 
 He argued that a market of 1.4 billion people should be treated as an opportunity to build globally competitive products, not as a guarantee that substandard goods will continue to find buyers. 
 The emphasis on quality also reflects the need to move beyond low-cost production towards globally competitive manufacturing standards. 
 Strengthening Domestic Manufacturing and Reducing Import Dependence 
 The Prime Minister identified several areas requiring greater investment: 
 Pharmaceuticals 
 Although India is known as the “Pharmacy of the World” for its finished medicines, it continues to import substantial quantities of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), bulk drugs and drug intermediates. 
 The industry was urged to invest in advanced technologies and large-scale production facilities to develop domestic capabilities in pharmaceutical ingredients. 
 Steel and Aluminium 
 India exports iron ore but continues to import certain grades of finished steel. 
 Similarly, despite possessing substantial bauxite reserves, India imports specialised aluminium alloys and related products. Developing domestic manufacturing capabilities in these segments could strengthen industrial self-reliance. 
 Agriculture and Food Processing 
 India’s share in global agricultural exports remains only 2-2.5%, despite its large agricultural base. 
 The Prime Minister urged corporates to increase investment in agriculture and food processing, establish dependable procurement systems and develop products according to the requirements of specific overseas markets. 
 Engineering Goods and Industrial Machinery 
 Indian companies were encouraged to explore global demand for engineering products, including packaging equipment, irrigation systems and factory-related machinery. 
 The Prime Minister also called upon larger companies to help smaller enterprises improve product quality, manufacturing scale and competitiveness. 
 Leveraging Free Trade Agreements and Global Markets 
 The Prime Minister urged FICCI to prepare a strategy for maximising opportunities arising from India’s free trade agreements (FTAs). 
 Businesses need to understand the requirements of international markets, identify products with export potential and develop manufacturing capabilities accordingly. 
 He emphasised an “India First” approach, encouraging businesses to look beyond domestic demand and prepare for global opportunities over the next two decades. 
 The broader objective is to strengthen India’s position in global value chains through higher-quality products, greater domestic value addition and competitive manufacturing.

 Corporate Responsibility FAQs 
 Q1. What did Prime Minister Narendra Modi criticise India Inc for? + 
 Ans . He criticised corporates for not adequately increasing employee salaries or employment despite receiving corporate tax reductions and other policy support. He also questioned the quality of products manufactured for Indian consumers.
 Q2. How was India's corporate tax rate reduced? + 
 Ans . The corporate tax rate was reduced from 30% in 2014 to 22% in 2019 for eligible domestic companies opting for the concessional tax regime.
 Q3. What is the Worker Population Ratio (WPR)? + 
 Ans . WPR is the proportion of the population that is employed. India's WPR for people aged 15 years and above increased from 46.8% in 2017-18 to 58.2% in 2023-24.
 Q4. What is informal employment? + 
 Ans . Informal employment generally refers to work that lacks adequate formal employment arrangements and social security benefits such as provident fund and medical insurance.
 Q5. Why is India dependent on imports in the pharmaceutical sector? + 
 Ans . Despite its strength in finished medicines, India continues to import significant quantities of APIs, bulk drugs and drug intermediates, highlighting gaps in domestic manufacturing capabilities.
